Chapter 6: Picking Up the Pieces
When the killing finally slows, Rwanda finds itself wrapped in a silence that feels even heavier than the violence ever did.
The city’s streets—once alive with laughter and everyday noise—are suddenly marked by absence. There are empty homes, abandoned markets, and the quiet, almost invisible grief of those who survived.
The peacekeepers are still there. But they’ve changed. You can see it in the way they move through the aftermath—each step carrying a sense of numbness.
And even though the gunfire has stopped, the real work is just beginning.
Imagine a local teacher—someone who once filled her classroom with stories and laughter. Now, she wanders through makeshift camps, calling out the names of her students, hoping just to spot a familiar face in the crowd.
Every reunion is a mix of relief and heartbreak, because for every child she finds, there are others still missing. The camps themselves are packed and tense, full of people who’ve lost everything they knew. Food’s scarce, medicine even more so, and disease creeps in quickly.
The mission’s headquarters turns into a sort of lifeline—organizing aid, distributing food, and trying to make sense of the chaos. More peacekeepers arrive, along with waves of humanitarian workers, all doing their best to bring some order.
They set up food lines, open up little clinics, and work tirelessly to help reunite families. But the needs just keep coming, and there’s never quite enough to go around.
One afternoon, a young doctor sits quietly with a child who won’t speak. The child’s eyes are distant, lost in memories too painful to share. The doctor offers gentle words, and even a small toy—hoping for just a flicker of connection.
It might seem like a small gesture, but in that moment, it feels like a lifeline. Sometimes, that’s all you can give.
Everyone carries their trauma in different ways. Some survivors are angry, demanding justice for all they’ve lost. Others turn inward, struggling to find any meaning in a world that’s been turned upside down.
The peacekeepers feel it too. At night, they gather together, swapping stories and trying to process everything they’ve seen. There’s a sense of failure that lingers, but also a quiet determination to help rebuild—no matter how long it takes.
And slowly, the first signs of recovery start to show. A market reopens. Hammers ring out as people patch up their homes. Children trickle back to school, their laughter tentative but genuine.
The road ahead is long, but the resilience of the Rwandan people is impossible to miss.
It becomes clear that healing is about more than just food or medicine. Trust needs to be rebuilt. Wounds—both the ones you can see and the ones you can’t—will take years to heal.
The peacekeepers, who once felt like outsiders, now find themselves deeply connected to Rwanda and its people.
They know, without a doubt, that their time here will stay with them forever.
